strengths: The paper addresses a useful, relatively underexplored vision task: editing an image using only a target emotion while retaining scene content. Several examples demonstrate meaningful changes beyond global color transfer.

EmoPair provides a potentially valuable training resource: 331,595 emotion-labeled InstructPix2Pix pairs and 6,949 additional generated pairs. The manuscript credits the underlying datasets and methods and commits to releasing its assets.

Human evaluation provides evidence beyond classifier scores. Figure 5 reports approximately 56% average preference for EmoEditor, including 60% against color transfer and 61% against single-word-prompted InstructPix2Pix. Component and iteration ablations are also provided.
The pipeline illustrations aid understanding, and the explicit discussion of failure cases, emotional manipulation risks, informed consent, and IRB approval is welcome.
weaknesses: The principal quantitative evidence is confounded by reuse of the same emotion predictor P for dataset labeling/filtering, inference selection, and evaluation through EMR, ESR, and ENRD. Table 1 shows EMR falling from 50.20% to 5.06% without the critic. This makes it essential to distinguish improved editing from improved performance against the selection model. Independent human evaluation of these ablations and baselines receiving the same critic and generation budget are missing.

The baseline configuration does not establish a convincing advantage over competitive alternatives. InstructPix2Pix and CLIP-Styler receive single emotion words despite the manuscript explicitly identifying such prompts as ineffective. LMS partly addresses this concern, but the cited Affective Image Filter is not evaluated. A baseline fine-tuned on the same EmoPair data would also help isolate the proposed method's contribution.

The independent human evidence is considerably weaker than the broad superiority claims. Figure S7 reports 54% preference over LMS online, 50% for negative-to-positive online edits, and 49% overall in the lab. The study measures relative emotional preference without assessing source-content preservation. Only 27% of online participants pass screening, and the aggregation underlying the reported standard errors is insufficiently specified. The stated 417,000 trials is also a correctable arithmetic error: 417 participants completing 100 trials yields 41,700 before exclusions.

Technical originality and reasoning claims are overstated. The global/local branches closely resemble the image and text conditioning of the pretrained InstructPix2Pix backbone. Moreover, the emotion encoder receives only a category label, so every image with the same target emotion receives the same embedding. Aligning that embedding with diverse instruction embeddings does not itself demonstrate source-specific instruction reasoning or a neuro-symbolic mechanism. Comparisons with simpler learned emotion embeddings are needed.

Dataset validity and semantic preservation are insufficiently established. Most pairs receive automatic emotion labels from a predictor with 73% accuracy on EmoSet; its labeling accuracy on the synthetic data is not audited. The SSIM/LPIPS filters do not guarantee semantic consistency, and Figure S3 includes substantial subject replacement, such as a dog becoming a toy house. Human validation of emotional transitions and retained content would materially strengthen this contribution. Same-valence and neutral-image generalization are supported only by selected examples.

Important technical definitions and implementation details require clarification. Section 3.2 constructs the noisy training latent from the source image and never introduces the paired target latent, making the written objective appear to train source reconstruction. ESR uses KL divergence from a predicted distribution to a one-hot target, which is generally infinite without an unstated convention or smoothing. Section S2.2 also omits learning rate, batch size, training duration, and sampling/guidance settings. These may be documentation errors, but they currently obstruct verification and reproduction.
